n: The topic of this lecture is the determination of metal cations in the mineralisate, namely arsenic and mercury. According to the plan, we first consider arsenic-containing compounds and their toxicological significance, then the methods for separating arsenic from the mineralisate and analysing it. For mercury, we study its uses, signs of poisoning, destruction of the specimen, determination of mercury in the destructate, and granosan.

Uses of arsenic compounds. As2O3, that is, arsenic trioxide, is used in medicine, in particular in dentistry, in agriculture as an insecticide, and in glass and leather production. Davidov's preparation, Schweinfurt green and Paris green are highly effective insecticides. Of the organic compounds, novarsenol and osarsol are used in medicine. Lewisite, adamsite and AsH3 may be used as toxic weapons.

The toxic action of arsenic. Pentavalent compounds are converted in the body into the more toxic trivalent compounds. Water-soluble compounds are rapidly absorbed from the blood, bind to the sulfhydryl groups of enzymes and disrupt their work. As a result, metabolism in the body stops, the capillaries are paralysed and necroses form.

Accumulation and elimination of arsenic. Arsenic accumulates in the body in the parenchymatous organs, bones, skin and hair. It is eliminated in the urine, through the intestines and through glands, but elimination is very slow. Therefore arsenic can be detected in a cadaver even after several years.

t: Arsenic: lethal dose and types of poisoning
n: The lethal dose of arsenic and types of poisoning. The lethal dose of white arsenic, that is, As2O3, is from 0.06 g to 0.2 g. Of cases of poisoning with arsenic compounds, 50% end in death. There are two types of poisoning: paralytic, when a large amount is rapidly absorbed, and poisoning via the gastrointestinal tract. The method of determining arsenic in specimens for forensic chemical analysis was discovered in 1836 by the English scientist Marsh.

t: Separating arsenic and the analysis scheme
n: Separating arsenic and the analysis scheme. Mineralisation with sulphuric and nitric acids makes it possible to recover 40-60% of the arsenic. The methods are: the Zanger-Black, silver diethyldithiocarbamate and Marsh reactions. The analysis begins with the mineralisate: first the preliminary Zanger-Black reaction, then the Marsh reaction, examination of the stain and quantification. Remember: the Zanger-Black reaction has negative significance; if no reaction appears, the examination is stopped.

The principle of the Zanger-Black reaction. Arsenic compounds are reduced to AsH3 and allowed to act on paper impregnated with mercuric chloride or bromide. Reduction proceeds by means of nascent hydrogen: Zn + H2SO4 -> ZnSO4 + 2H. To speed up the reaction, the zinc is copper-plated. 5-valent arsenic is reduced with difficulty, so the process is carried out in the presence of Fe(II) and Sn(II). The AsH3 formed gives a yellow stain with HgBr2.

Reducing arsenic(V). 5-valent arsenic is reduced with more difficulty than 3-valent arsenic, so the reaction is carried out in the presence of Fe(II) and Sn(II) compounds. First stage: AsO4(2-) + Sn(2+) + 4H+ -> AsO2(-) + Sn(4+) + 2H2O. Next stage: AsO2(-) + 7H -> AsH3 + 2H2O. Reduction proceeds by means of nascent hydrogen: Zn + H2SO4 -> ZnSO4 + 2H.

The procedure of the Zanger-Black reaction. Into the flask of the apparatus are placed 2 ml of mineralisate, 10 ml of 4 N H2SO4, 5 ml of water and 1 ml of 10% SnCl2, that is, a solution in 50% H2SO4. Then 2 g of pieces of copper-plated zinc are added. The flask is closed with a special stopper from which hang cotton wool impregnated with lead acetate and filter paper impregnated with mercuric bromide. If arsenic is present, a yellow-brown stain forms. To see it more clearly, the filter paper is dipped into a 3% KI solution.

Stain formation in the Zanger-Black reaction. AsH3 reacts stepwise with HgCl2 or HgBr2 and gives a yellow or brown stain on the paper. The final product is written in the book as As2Hg3. When KI is added, the reactions HgCl2 + 2KI -> HgI2 + 2KCl and HgI2 + 2KI -> K2[HgI4] take place. H2S formed from H2SO4, that is, H2SO4 + 8H -> H2S + 4H2O, is retained as PbS by the cotton wool with lead acetate.

The reaction with silver diethyldithiocarbamate. 2 g of copper-plated zinc is placed in the flask. Into the dropping funnel are placed 10 ml of mineralisate, 5 ml of water and 1 ml of 10% SnCl2. The bent end of the gas delivery tube is dipped into a solution of silver diethyldithiocarbamate in pyridine. The AsH3 formed gives a red or pink colour with silver diethyldithiocarbamate.

We compare three methods of determining arsenic. In the Zanger-Black method, a yellow-brown stain forms on filter paper with HgBr2; a negative result has forensic chemical significance. A solution of silver diethyldithiocarbamate in pyridine gives a red or pink colour with AsH3. In the Marsh method, a shiny black stain forms in the narrow part of the heated tube.

t: Marsh reaction: three stages and apparatus
n: The Marsh reaction consists of three stages. Arsenic is converted into volatile AsH3, and on heating a stain forms in the tube. The three stages are: purity of the reagents, determination from the mineralisate, and authenticity of the stain. The apparatus consists of a 150 ml flask, a dropping funnel, a calcium chloride tube and the Marsh tube.

The Marsh apparatus and safety. The apparatus has 3 parts: a 150 ml flask with a dropping funnel, a tube with CaCl2, and the reducing Marsh tube. The flask contains 10 g of copper-plated zinc. 3-4 ml of acid must always be left in the funnel: if air gets into the tube, the apparatus may explode on heating. The widened part of the tube is wrapped with metal gauze, and the narrow part is cooled with a wet wick. The stain forms precisely in the narrow part.

t: Marsh: checking the purity of reagents
n: Checking the purity of reagents in the Marsh reaction. 10 g of copper-plated zinc is placed in the flask, and anhydrous calcium chloride is placed in the calcium chloride tube. 30 ml of 10% H2SO4 is poured into the funnel and added dropwise to the flask containing the copper-plated zinc; 3-4 ml must always be left in the funnel. After 20-30 minutes it is checked that no air remains in the tube. When the hydrogen coming out of the end of the tube is ignited, the flame must not turn blue. If a shiny black stain forms when the tube is heated, the reagent is unfit.

Analysis of the mineralisate by the Marsh method. To the 10 g of copper-plated zinc in the Marsh flask, 30 ml of 4 N H2SO4 is added in small portions from the funnel. To the flask are added 20 ml of mineralisate and 2 ml of 10% SnCl2 in 50% H2SO4. The widened part of the tube is heated, and the narrow part is cooled with a wick of wet gauze. After 20-30 minutes the presence of arsenic is checked.

We repeat the key quantities in the Marsh method. 10 g of copper-plated zinc is placed in the flask. To check the purity of the reagents, 30 ml of 10% H2SO4 is poured into the funnel. In the analysis of the mineralisate, 20 ml of mineralisate and 2 ml of 10% SnCl2, that is, a solution in 50% H2SO4, are added. The waiting time is 20-30 minutes, after which the presence of arsenic is checked.

Signs of the Marsh stain. A shiny stain forms in the tube. The flame turns blue and a smell of garlic and onion is noticed; this is AsH3. If the burning flame is touched to a porcelain dish, a brown-grey stain forms. When the end of the tube is dipped into an ammoniacal solution of AgNO3, reduction of silver is observed.

The process in the Marsh reaction with an ammoniacal AgNO3 solution. When the end of the tube is dipped into an ammoniacal solution of AgNO3: AsH3 + 3AgNO3 -> AsAg3 + 3HNO3. Then AsAg3 + 3AgNO3 -> AsAg3·3AgNO3 is formed. Then AsAg3·3AgNO3 + 3H2O -> 6Ag + H3AsO3 + 3HNO3. That is, silver is reduced. The HNO3 released combines with ammonia.

t: Authenticity of the Marsh stain: arsenic and antimony
n: We check the authenticity of the Marsh stain for arsenic and antimony. When heated in air, arsenic gives octahedral crystals and antimony gives an amorphous precipitate. If the stain is dissolved in NaOCl solution, arsenic dissolves and antimony does not. If 5 N HCl and CsCl are added to the residue dissolved in HNO3, antimony gives colourless polyhedral crystals and arsenic does not.

t: Marsh stain: dissolving in HNO3 and the CsCl test
n: Dissolving the Marsh stain in HNO3 and the CsCl test. The stain is dissolved in HNO3: 3As + 5HNO3 + 2H2O -> 3H3AsO4 and 3Sb + 5HNO3 -> 3HSbO3 + 5NO + H2O. The solution is dried on a microscope slide. If 1 drop of 5 N HCl and a crystal of CsCl are added to the residue, antimony gives colourless polyhedral crystals. Arsenic gives no crystals with CsCl, but when CsCl + KI is added, it gives a red-orange precipitate.

Quantitative determination of arsenic. In the argentometric method, the AsH3 formed is passed through an ammoniacal solution of AgNO3. The excess AgNO3 is titrated with NH4CNS using ferric ammonium sulphate as indicator. In the colorimetric method, the stain is determined by comparison, based on the Zanger-Black reaction. In the silver diethyldithiocarbamate method, AsH3 is passed through its solution in pyridine, and the red-pink colour formed is determined colorimetrically.

t: Uses of mercury and its compounds
n: Now, the uses of mercury and its compounds. Mercury and its compounds are used in engineering, in the chemical industry, in agriculture and in medicine. In metallic form, in medicine, it is used in preparing ointments, and in thermometers and instruments; metallic mercury is of low toxicity. HgCl2, that is, corrosive sublimate, is used as a disinfectant and a reagent, and corrosive sublimate in particular has a strong action. Organic mercury compounds, for example granosan, are used as pesticides.

Mercury poisoning. Mercury enters as dust with respiration and first of all damages the cerebral cortex. It binds to sulfhydryl groups and disrupts physiological functions. Mercury compounds taken in with food damage the stomach, liver, kidneys and various functional glands; haemorrhages occur in the organs and bloody diarrhoea develops. Mercury accumulates in the liver and kidneys, and in chronic poisoning kidney disease develops. It is eliminated from the body slowly: mainly in the urine, faeces, through the skin, and through the salivary and mammary glands.

Route of entry, target organs and elimination in mercury poisoning. Mercury as dust enters by inhalation, and its compounds with food. Target organs: the cerebral cortex, stomach, liver and kidneys. Mercury accumulates in the liver and kidneys. It is eliminated slowly, mainly in the urine, faeces, through the skin, and through the salivary and mammary glands. In chronic poisoning, kidney disease is observed.

The clinical picture of mercury poisoning. Severe stomach pain, nausea, vomiting, a metallic taste and white patches in the mouth appear, and sometimes diarrhoea occurs. Blood appears in the urine, and the kidneys fail rapidly. In time, cardiac activity weakens. At autopsy in mercury poisoning, especially in the kidneys, corrosive sublimate nephrosis is clearly visible.

t: Mercury is lost in mineralisation: destruction
n: Mercury is lost in mineralisation, therefore destruction is used. In poisoning with mercury compounds, when the specimen is mineralised by the dry and wet methods, almost all the mercury is lost. Therefore, for the determination of mercury, the method of destruction of the specimen has been proposed; this is Vasilyeva's method. Destruction is the incomplete burning of the specimen, or the breaking down of connective tissues with nitric acid, sulphuric acid and other oxidising agents.

The difference between mineralisation and destruction. In dry and wet mineralisation almost all the mercury is lost, so the specimen is subjected to destruction. Destruction is the incomplete burning of the specimen, or the breaking down of connective tissues with nitric acid, sulphuric acid and other oxidising agents. In the destructate, protein is partly broken down and remains in the form of peptide bonds. A small amount of ethyl alcohol acts as a catalyst.

t: Composition of the destructate and removal of excess HNO3
n: Composition of the destructate and removal of excess HNO3. Mercury is bound to sulfhydryl groups; on superficial oxidation it passes into the inorganic state. In the destructate, mercury ions are mixed with proteins, peptides, amino acids and lipids. To speed things up, a little ethyl alcohol is added. Excess HNO3 is removed with saturated urea: N2, CO2 and H2O are released.

Destruction of liver and kidney. Liver and kidney are taken separately, 20 g each. To the organ in the flask are added 5 ml of water, 1 ml of ethyl alcohol, 10 ml of conc. HNO3, then dropwise 10 ml of conc. H2SO4. After the acids are added, the flask is heated for 5-10 minutes at room temperature and for 10-20 minutes in a boiling water bath. If the reaction becomes too vigorous, 20-30 ml of boiling water is added to the flask. The destructate is filtered while hot, the residue is washed with hot water, 20 ml of urea solution is added, and the volume is made up to the mark.

t: Determining mercury in urine and blood
n: Determining mercury in urine and blood. Mercury is excreted by the kidneys in the urine; A.F. Rubtsov and A.N. Krylova proposed two methods. Method 1: in a Kjeldahl flask, to 200 ml of urine are added 35 ml of conc. HNO3, 2 ml of ethyl alcohol and 25 ml of conc. H2SO4; 40 minutes on a water bath, then 20 ml of saturated thiourea. Method 2: to 200 ml of urine are added 25 ml of conc. H2SO4 and 7 g of KMnO4 and the mixture is stirred for 40 minutes; saturated oxalic acid is added until the colour disappears. Mercury in blood is determined as in liver and kidney, except that water is not added.

Determining mercury with dithizone. To half of the destructate in a separating funnel, 10 ml of chloroform is added, the mixture is shaken for 1 minute, and the layer is discarded. This last portion is repeated until it is colourless. To the purified destructate are added 10 ml of 10% ascorbic acid, 5 ml of chloroform and 0.3 ml of a 0.01% chloroform solution of dithizone, and the mixture is shaken. If the chloroform layer takes on a yellow-orange colour, this indicates the presence of mercury.

Determining mercury with CuI suspension. When 10 ml of CuI suspension is added, a red-orange precipitate forms: Hg2+ + 4CuI -> Cu2[HgI4] + 2Cu+. Oxidising agents interfere with the reaction, because free I2 is released from CuI. The amount is determined photocolorimetrically as the dithizonate, and colorimetrically as Cu2[HgI4].

t: Mercury: comparing the dithizone and CuI methods
n: We compare two methods of determining mercury. In the dithizone method, if ascorbic acid and dithizone are added to the purified destructate, the chloroform layer becomes yellow-orange; the amount is determined by photocolorimetry. In the CuI suspension method, a red-orange precipitate of Cu2[HgI4] forms; the amount is determined by colorimetry. Oxidising agents interfere, because free I2 is released from CuI.

Granosan and its action. Granosan is a mixture of 2% ethylmercuric chloride, a dye, a mineral acid and talc; depending on its composition it is also marketed under the names mercusan and mercurhexan. As a toxic chemical it is used for dressing cotton seed and other seeds before sowing. It acts by absorption through the skin and accumulates in the body. It sharply reduces the number of erythrocytes, impairs liver function and inflames the skin. Ethylmercuric chloride is a white crystalline substance melting at 192°C; it is sparingly soluble in water and readily soluble in hot ethyl alcohol, acetone and alkali.

Separating granosan from the specimen. Cadaver organs and plant parts are steeped 2 times with 3 N HCl for 30-60 minutes, and the liquid is extracted 2 times with chloroform. Urine is acidified with conc. HCl and extracted with chloroform after 30 minutes. Alkali is added to blood and it is heated for 10 minutes on a water bath. HCl is added to the clear liquid, the mixture is stirred for 15 minutes, centrifuged and separated with chloroform.

There are two ways to determine granosan. With copper wire: metallic copper displaces mercury from ethylmercuric chloride. The silvery coating is dissolved in a solution of iodine in KI and determined as Cu2HgI4. In thin-layer chromatography, that is, TLC, acetate buffer, pH = 4.5, water and dithizone are added to the extract, and the yellow dithizonate is transferred into chloroform. The residue is dissolved in 0.5-1 ml of chloroform and spotted on a plate. In the n-heptane-chloroform 2:5 system, the yellow spot is identified by its Rf.

The copper wire reaction of granosan. Metallic copper displaces mercury from ethylmercuric chloride, and the liberated mercury is deposited on the copper. The silvery coating is dissolved with a solution of iodine in KI and determined as Cu2HgI4: HgI2 + 2KI -> K2HgI4. Then K2HgI4 + 10KI reacts with 6CuSO4 and 3Na2SO3 to form Cu2[HgI4]. Excess I2 is neutralised with Na2SO3, and HI with bicarbonate.

We compare arsenic and mercury. Arsenic is determined from the mineralisate as AsH3; the methods are Zanger-Black and Marsh. Because mercury is lost in mineralisation, it is determined from the destructate with dithizone and CuI. Organic mercury, that is, granosan, is steeped with HCl, extracted into chloroform and examined with copper wire and by TLC.

Let us summarise. Arsenic is determined as AsH3: first the preliminary Zanger-Black reaction, then the Marsh reaction, and the authenticity of the stain is checked. For mercury, liver and kidney are destroyed separately, and excess HNO3 is removed with urea. Mercury is determined with dithizone and CuI suspension; granosan is extracted into chloroform and examined by TLC. For self-check, revise: the stages of the Marsh test, distinguishing the stain as arsenic or antimony, and the essence of destruction.
